sentences.text: Hello. I'm Gill at engVid, and today's lesson is a rather advanced lesson on word order changes, also known as word order inversion, which happens after certain words and phrases, which we have in red here on the left. And this is something that it's a little bit unusual

- it sounds a bit strange, it's a rather almost poetic kind of style, something that you'd see more in writing than in speaking. If people spoke like this, it would sound a little bit unusual, a little bit strange, unless they're actors in a play that was written

100 years ago or more, then you would hear that sort of thing. And also, if you're reading a novel or a story that was written quite a long time ago, you might see these kinds of word orders written in the story, in a book. So, it's a useful thing to know about,
and if you ever need to use it yourself, it's a useful thing to be able to do if you want to write in a certain style.
So, okay, so let's have a look at the examples.

So, if you start a sentence with "never", that's when you have to change the word order, and instead of saying... If you started with "I", "I have never seen", then it's "I have never seen". But if you start the sentence with "never", maybe for emphasis, it's more dramatic in a way. "Never have I seen", and

it's a sort of strong, dramatic statement. So, "Never have I seen", rather than "Never I have seen". So, you can start with "I have", "I have never seen", but if you start the sentence with "never", you have to change the order of "I have" to "have I". "Never
have I seen such a lovely flower." Okay? So, this is the same kind of idea all the way through where we're reversing some of the words.
So, similarly then, "Only then did I realize".

I suppose if you're... If you're not going to start the sentence with "only then", you'd say, "I realized then who she was", and then you don't even need the auxiliary verb "did", but because we've started "only then", "Did I realize". So, "only then", you wouldn't

say, "Only then I realized", it doesn't sound quite right. You have to use "did" with it. "Only then did I realize who she was." If you meet somebody famous and you don't really recognize them at first, but then when the person begins to speak, oh, you recognize
the voice, and then, "Only then did I realize who she was." A famous actress, maybe. Okay.

Again, it's more dramatic. "Only then did I realize". Okay. So, then this one, "not only", and then with a "but" somewhere in the sentence. So, "Not only is she a singer, but she's an artist too." So, if you weren't beginning the sentence with "not only", you'd
say, "She is not only a singer, but also an artist", but that doesn't sound quite so good.
So, it sounds better to begin with "not only".

"Not only is she a singer", I think the order the words come in, the rhythm of it, the shape of it sounds better this way. "Not only is she a singer, but she's an artist too." So, the words kind of come at the right moment. It sounds better.

Okay, then this word, it's a bit unusual. "Seldom", but it means not often, not very often. So, "seldom" means not often. "Seldom have I heard such a beautiful song." So, you could start with "I have seldom heard", and you would have a different word order. So,

if you start with "seldom", you've got to have "I have" reversed instead of "I have seldom heard". It's "Seldom have I heard such a beautiful song", but that's a very sort of old-fashioned-sounding style. You would read it in a book, I think, or hear it in
a play that was written many years ago, but you wouldn't hear people saying it, I don't think, in... Nowadays, in everyday conversation.

Okay, and the next one, "little". "Did I know how my life would change?" So, without "little", you would say "I didn't know", because "little" is a kind of negative. "I didn't know how my life would change", but "little did I know" is quite a dramatic way of saying it

when something... A big change happens in your life. "Little did I know when I walked into that room and met a certain person how my life would change." Okay. So, again, "little did I know" is a sort of rather dramatic way of speaking. Okay, next one, "in no way
can we agree to that". So, instead of just saying "we can't agree to that", this is much stronger. "In no way", it's much more definite.

"In no way can we agree to that", so quite dramatic really, and very strong emphasis saying "no way, no way, we're not going to do that". So, okay. And then similarly, "in no way" and "on no account" mean the same thing. So, "on no account should we sign that

contract", meaning we should not sign that contract. So, "on no account", there's the negative "no", "we should not", but "on no account should we", instead of "we should", "should we sign that contract". Okay?

Then, "only when I got home did I", again, we've got a "did", "did I" with "only then" and now "only when", "only when I got home did I realize what I'd done". So, how would you say it more normally? "I only realized when I got home what I'd done", but it doesn't

sound quite so good. "Only when I got home did I realize what I'd done". So, it's still a bit poetic, it doesn't sound really like everyday speaking. Okay. Right, and then "only by regular study can you", instead of "you can", "can you improve your English". So,

without starting here, you'd say "you can only improve your English by regular study", but starting with "only by", it's more... It gets your attention straight away. "Only by regular study can you improve your English." Okay.

So, next one, "no sooner", "no sooner had I left", instead of "I had left", it's "had I left". "No sooner had I left", left the house, perhaps, "when it began to rain". So, the more normal way of saying that would be just to say "as soon as I had left the house",
or "as soon as I left the house, it began to rain". So, "no sooner", it's a bit more poetic, I suppose. Okay. And then there's this one that you use instead of saying "if".
So, "if I had known", what would happen next?

"If I had known, I wouldn't have gone to that party." But instead of "if", you just start with "had I known", instead of using the word "if" at all. Instead of "I had known", it's "had I known". "Had I known what would happen next,

I wouldn't have gone to that party." Okay. So, I hope that's a useful way of perhaps expanding your knowledge of English and some unusual constructions that are perhaps a little bit old-fashioned or poetic, but things that you might recognize if you're reading a certain

type of book, like a novel, or reading a play, perhaps, where people are speaking in a certain style. So, if you'd like to do a quiz on this to test your knowledge, just go to the website, www.engvid.com, and give the quiz a try. And so, thank you for watching,
and hope to see you again soon. Bye for now.
